slot.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
slot.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain why letting the stick rebound keeps the hands relaxed

visuals.intent: A hand holding a drumstick in matched grip, seen so the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger is plain, for the Learner to copy.
The four moments of a full stroke in order, raised, striking, rebounding, and back at the starting height, so the Learner sees the stick come back up on its own.

lesson.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
lesson.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain that letting the stick rebound and keeping the hands relaxed are both part of the stroke

blocks.text: Imagine a stick striking a drum and bouncing back up, with your hand staying loose. As you work toward playing “Iris” from beginning to end, the focus here is a relaxed hold and a stroke that comes back up.

Matched grip means holding a stick the same way in each hand [1]. The fulcrum is the holding point between your thumb and index finger [2]. In matched grip, the stick rests inside the first knuckle of your index finger, with your thumb opposite it and pointing along the stick [1]. Your other fingers wrap loosely around the stick, and your hand stays relaxed rather than squeezing at the fulcrum [1].

sections.heading: A stroke that comes back up

blocks.text: For a full stroke—a hit that returns to its starting height—your wrist raises the stick above the drum [1]. The stick strikes the drum’s surface, then you let it bounce back naturally rather than stop it there [3]. Your fingers and wrist stay relaxed while your thumb and index finger maintain contact with the stick [3]. A full stroke is one smooth movement from high to the drum and back to the same height, without stopping points along the way [1][3].

Your other fingers wrap loosely around the stick, and your hand stays relaxed rather than squeezing at the fulcrum [src_498b43255b].

placement.section: A stroke that comes back up

brief.subject: A hand and drumstick pass through four moments of a full stroke above a drum.
mustShow: Four panels appear in order, labelled Raised, Striking, Bouncing back, and Back at starting height.
The first panel shows the stick raised above the drum.
The second panel shows the stick tip touching the drum’s surface.
The third panel shows an upward arrow beside the stick as it moves away from the drum.
The last panel shows the stick at the same height and angle as in the first panel.
brief.caption: The Course’s own schematic shows a full stroke from raised stick to strike and back to its starting height.
brief.alt: Four panels show a hand holding a stick above a drum: raised, touching the drum, bouncing upward with an arrow, and back at the original height and angle.

proposed.definition: A way of holding drumsticks with the same hand position in both hands.
The point where a drumstick is held and can pivot.
A drum hit in which the stick starts high and returns to the same height.

illustrations.subject: A hand and drumstick pass through four moments of a full stroke above a drum.
